en: The Ritual for Repentance According to the Brahmajāla Sūtra, Clarified by the Bodhisattva Precept Disciple Ouyi Zhixu.
The sūtra states: "If there are those who have violated the ten precepts, they should be instructed to perform repentance before the images of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas."
Recite the ten grave precepts and the forty-eight light precepts during the six periods of day and night; with utmost sincerity, prostrate before the thousand Buddhas of the three periods of time.
Whether for one week, two or three weeks, or even up to a year, you must seek a favorable sign (*lakṣaṇa*); only then will your transgressions be extinguished.

This is the explicit instruction from the Golden Mouth [of the Buddha]. Thus, one should know that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the *Vaipulya*, the *Mahākaruṇā*, the *Cen-ch'a* (Observation), and other such [scriptures]...

Although each of these methods for practicing the Dharma possesses the capacity to extinguish transgressions and attain precepts, for one who has violated the ten precepts, it is still necessary to specifically rely on the ritual procedures of the Brahma Net Sūtra (*Brahmajāla-sūtra*).
Only then will the focused resolve not become diffuse—what is called "falling back to the ground as if from a height."
He then rose from the ground. Furthermore, this sutra clarifies that even in a thousand-li area where no teacher is present, one may receive the precepts by oneself before an image;
it simply states that one should repent before the Buddha for seven days, and upon seeing a "good sign," one obtains the precepts.

If one does not see a good sign, one should continue for two weeks, three weeks, or even up to a year, until a good sign is obtained. It does not, however, say that one must practice with such extreme urgency.

Worshiping the thousand Buddhas of the three periods is essentially the same in its general intent as the self-vowed reception of the precepts found in the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra* (Yíngluò) and the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* (Dìchí).

Therefore, although I have already previously expounded upon the methods for studying and receiving the precepts, I now specifically clarify the ritual for repentance for those who have committed the ten grave offenses after receiving the Bodhisattva precepts, so that they may, by relying on the Buddhas of the three periods, be cleared of their transgressions. This having been seen...

If auspicious signs appear, the essence of the precepts will be fully restored. Although one may not be fit for the communal functions within the *bhikṣu* dharma, one may become a bodhisattva śrāmaṇera or a bodhisattva upāsaka; thus, one may possess a sense of shame and virtue.

Furthermore, to secretly and silently advance on the Path and directly realize non-arising (*anutpāda*) is certainly not beyond one's capacity. This applies even to those with the eight or five precepts, and...

Regarding a śrāmaṇera who has violated a root precept: if he relies on this method of repentance and, having seen auspicious signs, obtains the Bodhisattva Great Precepts, it is likewise permissible for him to proceed to the bhikṣu precepts. As for a Hīnayāna bhikṣu who has violated a root precept:
Having performed this repentance and perceived auspicious signs, one secretly attains non-arising (*anutpāda*). Alternatively, it may be appended to the section on study.

Even if one’s obstacles are deep and a responsive resonance has not yet been achieved, by forever severing the continuity [of afflictions] and earnestly seeking compassion, one will surely be able to close the gates to the evil realms and plant the seeds for transcendence. This is briefly set forth in ten points: first, adorning the ritual site; second, ...
1. Purify the three karmas. 2. Offer the three kinds of incense and flowers. 3. Praise, prostrate, and take refuge. 4. Confess and eliminate transgressions.
5. Make vows and recite the precepts. 6. Prostrate with utmost sincerity to the Buddha. 7. Re-cultivate vows and practices. 8. Circumambulate and return to self-refuge.
Tenth, regarding the practice of mindfulness of the true nature while seated:
first, adorn the site of enlightenment by selecting a quiet and secluded hall or room; sweep and sprinkle it until it is pure and clean; and within it, install an image of Vairocana or Śākyamuni.
Furthermore, it is also permissible to install images of various bodhisattvas; however, there must be an image of the Buddha as the principal figure.
One should hang up banners, canopies, silken streamers, and flowers, providing all manner of adornments. One must exhaust one's own wealth and devote one's whole heart and full effort to this task.
Practice this with utmost sincerity; do not act with negligence or superficiality. Furthermore, do not readily solicit donations from patrons;
only when they are truly impoverished and have no means of support may you seek to provide for the task according to circumstances.

The practitioner who purifies the three karmas reflects to himself: "Because of past wholesome roots, I have fortunately been able to receive the precepts in this life. Yet, due to the obstruction of evil, I have again committed transgressions.
Since I have violated the pure precepts established by the Buddhas of the three periods of time, I am now [a transgressor]."
The beings in hell give rise to great shame and remorse; they give rise to great fear, as if dwelling in a latrine.
With single-minded resolve, they seek an exit, as if imprisoned in a jail, they seek liberation. They cannot entertain a single thought of worldly affairs for even a moment.
Having bathed until pure and donned fresh, clean garments, they maintain a sincere and devout will, their mouths free from idle chatter, as if holding a vessel full of oil, fearing its spilling.
As the drops fall, one should practice alone with single-minded diligence, seeking no companions.

Even if there should be one or two others who have likewise committed transgressions, they must first feel shame and apprehension and resolve their will with determination; only then may they practice together.

One must take the attainment of a favorable sign as the deadline, whether it be seven days, fourteen days, or even a year, or until the end of one’s life, without allowing the mind to slacken in the interim.
Regarding the offering of the three types of incense and flowers:
when the practitioner first arrives before the image, they should bring to mind all the Triple Gem of the ten directions, whose nature is identical to empty space and which is omnipresent.
Due to my own karmic obscurations, I do not see or know them; yet the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are ever-present toward me.
The sins I have committed and my current practices are all known and seen by them without exception.
It is like a blind person in a great assembly: though the blind person does not see the assembly, the assembly sees the blind person.
I am just like this; shrouded by ignorance, I have transgressed the prohibitions and precepts within the essence of the pure Dharma-realm, committing extreme offenses.
These grave offenses have long been seen and known by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. Today, having attained awakening, I feel shame, fear, and repentance for my transgressions.
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas will surely manifest before me, knowing and seeing me.

Having first given rise to such profound faith and understanding, one should regard the Triple Gem of the ten directions as if it were right before one's eyes. Arranging one’s seat and standing upright, one should chant aloud:
With all reverence, single-mindedly prostrate to the eternally abiding Triple Gem of the ten directions.
Having performed this single general prostration, burn incense, hold flowers, kneel with the right knee on the ground, and chant:
Respectfully holding incense and flowers, make offerings according to the Dharma.
May these clouds of incense and flowers pervade the worlds of the ten directions, making offerings to all the Buddhas,
the Honored Dharma, and the Bodhisattvas, as well as the infinite assembly of Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Rishis.
Within boundless Buddha-lands, they perform the work of Buddhas; universally perfuming all sentient beings, they cause them all to resolve upon Bodhicitta.
Then, scattering flowers with the hands, one further contemplates: "May these incense and flowers of mine pervade the ten directions as something sublime."
The Radiant Terrace, with the celestial music and precious celestial incense of the devas; the celestial delicacies and precious celestial garments;
and the inconceivable, wondrous dharmic atoms—each and every atom produces all atoms, and each and every atom produces all dharmas.
Whirling without obstruction, they mutually adorn one another, reaching universally before the Triple Gem in the ten directions.
Before the Triple Gem throughout the dharma-realm of the ten directions, my own body performs offerings; each and every one pervades the entire dharma-realm, distinct yet without hindrance.
Until the end of the future, they perform the work of Buddhas, universally permeating all sentient beings within the dharma-realm, so that they may receive [the benefit].
May all who are perfumed by this give rise to the bodhicitta and together enter the non-arising state to realize buddha-wisdom. Having visualized this, stand up and proclaim:
"The offering is completed; with all reverence, [one prostration]."
Having completed the practice of making offerings by praising, paying homage, and taking refuge, one should single-mindedly contemplate the true merits of the Triple Gem with longing and devotion,
vowing never to abandon them. Kneeling on the right knee with palms joined, one utters a Brahma-like voice and offers this praise:
The Tathāgata’s wondrous form-body is peerless in the world; it is incomparable and inconceivable, and for this reason I now pay homage.
The Tathāgata’s form is inexhaustible, and his wisdom is likewise so; all phenomena are eternally abiding.
Therefore, I take refuge in those who have well-tamed the faults of mind and body in its four aspects; because they have reached the inconceivable stage,
I now pay homage to them.
Knowing all such phenomena, your wisdom-body is unimpeded; because you have no forgetfulness regarding the Dharma, I now pay homage and prostrate to you who have transcended the immeasurable.
I prostrate to the peerless one; I prostrate to the sovereign of the Dharma.
I prostrate to the One who transcends thought,
who out of compassion protects me, causing the seeds of the Dharma to increase, so that until my final body,
I may always remain before the Tathāgata.
Whatever meritorious deeds I have cultivated in this life and in other births, by the power of these roots of goodness,
may the Buddha always accept me with his compassion.
(This verse is from the forty-eighth assembly of the *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra*, the "Assembly of Queen Śrīmālā").
Having finished the praise, perform one prostration. Rising, chant:
"With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to all Buddhas of the past throughout the limits of the past.
As you descend into prostration, contemplate: "The nature of both the one who bows and the object of worship is empty and quiescent; the resonance between cause and response is inconceivable. I..."
This site of enlightenment is like a constant wish-fulfilling jewel. Within the reflections of all Buddhas, my own body’s reflection appears before them;

with head touching their feet, I take refuge and pay homage. When reaching the point of "paying homage to the worthy sages," change the two characters for "Buddhas" (諸佛) to the two characters for "worthy sages" (賢聖).
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to all Buddhas of the future throughout the limits of the future.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to all Buddhas of the present throughout the limits of the present.
With single-minded devotion, prostrate to all the Honored Dharmas throughout the limits of the past. Contemplate thus:
"The Dharma-nature of true emptiness is like space; the eternally abiding Jewel of Dharma is inconceivable. My own body and shadow appear before this Jewel of Dharma;
with single-minded devotion, I take refuge and pay homage according to the Dharma."
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate to all the venerable Dharmas of the future world throughout the limits of the future.
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate to all the venerable Dharmas of the present world throughout the limits of the present.
I prostrate with my whole heart to all the worthy and holy ones of the past throughout the entirety of the past;
I prostrate with my whole heart to all the worthy and holy ones of the future throughout the entirety of the future.
With single-minded devotion, prostrate to all the worthy and holy ones of the present age, from this moment until the end of the present aeon.
Having performed one prostration to each, kneel with the right knee on the ground and recite:
"I, the disciple [Name], from this time forth until the end of the future, take refuge in the Buddha; I take refuge in the Dharma; I take refuge in the..."
Taking refuge in the Sangha of noble ones; taking refuge in the True Dharma and the Precepts.

Having recited this three times, bow once, and prostrate while visualizing as follows: "I and all sentient beings have, since beginningless time, been constantly obstructed by the grave offenses of the three karmas and six sense faculties.
We have not seen the Buddhas and do not know the essential path to liberation; we merely follow the flow of birth."
I died without knowing the sublime principle. Although I know it now, I am still hindered by all manner of grave transgressions, just like all sentient beings.
Now, before Śākyamuni and the Buddhas of the ten directions, I universally take refuge and repent on behalf of all sentient beings.
I pray only that you will grant your protection and cause these hindrances to be extinguished.

Having completed the fivefold confession of transgressions, the repentance for their removal, the taking of refuge, and the visualization, one should next kneel with the right knee on the ground and join the palms. Then, one should make this proclamation:
"For the sake of all sentient beings throughout the entire Dharma-realm, I vow to sever and eliminate the three obstructions; I now perform this sincere repentance."

Having chanted this, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground and further reflected: "From beginningless time until now, both I and all sentient beings, due to craving and false views, have:
(1) internally clung to a self and persons; (2) externally associated with evil friends; (3) failed to rejoice in even a hair’s breadth of another's merit;
and (4) throughout our three karmic doors, extensively committed manifold transgressions. Although these acts were not numerous, the evil intent was pervasive."
1. To spread [evil deeds] (5). 2. To continue day and night without interruption (6). 3. To conceal and deny one's faults, not wishing for others to know them (7).
4. To have no fear of the evil realms (8). 5. To lack shame and dread of blame (9). 6. To repudiate cause and effect (10).
Therefore, on this day, I now deeply believe in cause and effect (1), give rise to profound shame and dread (2), and experience great terror (3), and I openly confess and repent.

4. Regret; 5. severing the continuity of the mind; 6. generating the bodhicitta and abandoning evil while cultivating good; 7. diligently exerting the three karmas to overturn past grave transgressions; 8.
rejoicing in even a hair’s breadth of merit belonging to ordinary beings or sages; and 9. mindfulness of the Buddhas of the ten directions.
Possessing great merit and wisdom, you are able to rescue and deliver me and all sentient beings from the sea of the two deaths and place us upon the shore of the three virtues (9).
Since beginningless time, we have been ignorant of the fact that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty and quiescent; thus, we have extensively committed various evils.
Now, knowing this emptiness and quiescence, for the sake of seeking Bodhi and for the sake of sentient beings, we shall extensively cultivate all manner of goodness and universally sever all evils.
(10). I only pray that Vairocana Buddha and all World-Honored Ones will compassionately accept me and grant me audience for my repentance.

Having brought forth these ten minds of accordance and opposition, one should next kneel with the right knee on the ground and join the palms to confess and reveal the transgressions of violating the precepts.

Seeking out all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas currently dwelling in the worlds throughout the ten directions, with great compassion, may they wash me clean and cause me to attain purity once more. Weeping and wailing, he spoke thus.
I, disciple [Name], with a sincere heart, repent. Myself and all sentient beings are pure by nature, yet being shrouded by ignorance, we fail to realize this.
For these causes and conditions, we have long been submerged in birth and death. Now, fortunately encountering the True Dharma, I have received and uphold the Vinaya precepts;
yet my mind, distracted by afflictions, has again violated the rules of training and committed such [offenses]—whether it be taking life, stealing, or [whatever offense was committed].

Whether it be sexual misconduct or false speech (as explained according to the specific circumstances), such shameless dharmas cause one to be forever cast out from the ocean of the Buddha’s teachings.

One shall fall into the great Avīci hell, where fierce fires blaze and one undergoes immeasurable suffering; furthermore, one will pass through the various evil realms until there is no prospect of liberation.
Such karmic obstacles ensure that the law of cause and effect is never in vain.
All Buddhas and Bodhisattvas know me and see me; I now confess and reveal my faults, not daring to conceal them.

Raising a mind of rectitude and abandoning all deceitful conduct, I stand before all Tathāgatas of the ten directions and the assembly of Bodhisattvas who have entered the Great Stages, and with no regard for body or life, I repent of my transgressions.
I beg for mercy. May all sentient beings together wash away their past karma; may everything previously committed be entirely eliminated.
From this day forward, I vow never to create it again.
I pray that all Buddhas and great Bodhisattvas, through their great compassion, will take pity on me, uproot the seeds of my transgressions, and bestow upon me...
Regarding the pure precepts, one must complete the three recitations; then, rising to one's feet, one should announce:
"Repentance is finished," and prostrate once before the Triple Gem.

Having completed the confession and purification for those who have established the six vows and practice the recitation of the precepts, one should contemplate that offenses have no inherent nature; since they arise from conditions, they likewise cease through conditions.

Once the evils of offense have been extinguished, one is fit to abide in the Bodhisattva’s Threefold Pure Precepts (*tri-skandha-śīla*). Then, kneeling with the right knee on the ground and joining the palms:

Having made this formal announcement (*jñapti*), one looks up and addresses the Tathāgatas of the ten directions and the assembly of Bodhisattvas who have entered the great stages: "From this day forth, I..."
Until the end of the future, I vow never to retreat or abandon the great aspiration for Bodhi. I vow never to be separated from the three clusters of pure precepts.
I pray that throughout the boundless and limitless worlds of the ten directions, all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas—the foremost, true, and holy ones—[will grant their witness].
"I, [Name], earnestly pray that you will receive and uphold the pure precepts and codes of discipline, acting as witnesses for me all together.
Having made this announcement, one should recite the ten grave and forty-eight light precepts with utmost sincerity.

While reciting aloud, the mind should focus on the words and their meaning, ensuring there is no distraction. If one is unable to recite them in full at a single time, they may be divided into two sessions.
It is also permissible to recite one full cycle together during three sessions, or even up to six sessions.

When the seven prostrations have been completed, the practitioner follows along with the recitation of the precepts as much as possible; once it is finished, they prostrate, rise, add incense, and pay their respects with single-minded devotion.
Contemplating the Buddhas of the three periods of time as if they were standing before one’s eyes, with profound reverence and earnest sincerity, prostrate to each one.
With single-minded devotion, prostrate to Vairocana Buddha, the Teacher of the Brahma Net Sūtra (three prostrations).
With single-minded devotion, prostrate to the Original Teacher, Śākyamuni Buddha.
Next, prostrate to the three thousand Buddhas of the three periods of time, offering one prostration for each Buddha, or performing one hundred prostrations at each session.

One may perform eighty-five, fifty, forty-three, or thirty prostrations; it may also be according to one's capacity, whether more or less, provided that they are performed continuously without interruption.

Once one section has been completed, if no auspicious signs have been obtained, one should perform another section, continuing up to ten or even a hundred sections, making the attainment of auspicious signs the sole goal. Furthermore, if the practitioner’s physical strength and vitality are robust, they are able to...
Within seven days, perform one complete cycle of prostrations to three thousand Buddhas.
It is most excellent to continue in this manner for each subsequent seven-day period without interruption. If that is not possible, it is also acceptable to complete one cycle in two weeks.
Following this sequence, perform as many prostrations as you wish until the cycle is finished. Next, perform one final collective prostration and say:
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate to all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time.
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate to the subtle and honored Dharma of the "Bodhisattva Ground" chapter of the Brahma Net Sūtra (three prostrations).
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate to the Vinaya-piṭaka of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, and to all the honored Dharmas of the ten directions and the three periods of time.
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate to the Bodhisattva Lord of Mysterious Penetration and Flower Radiance, and to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Great Wisdom Light, King of Flower Radiance.

With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to Maitreya Bodhisattva, who is in his last birth before Buddhahood, and to all the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas of the ten directions and the three periods of time.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the Venerable Upāli, the Great Master of the Vinaya, and to all the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
The noble Sangha. One should understand that the visualization verses are as previously explained.
Eighth, the renewed cultivation of vows and practices.
After the practitioner has completed the prostrations to the Triple Gem, they add incense to pay their respects, kneel with the right knee on the ground, and join their palms.
Following the subtle and supreme practices cultivated by Maitreya Bodhisattva in the past, they face the Triple Gem as if it were present before their eyes and recite these words:
I now take refuge and pay homage to all the Buddhas of the ten directions; I also pay homage to the assembly of Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, and Great Sages who possess the divine eye.
The mind of enlightenment (bodhicitta) causes one to leave behind all evil realms and enables one to be born in the heavens above.
Even until the realization of nirvana,
whatever slight transgressions I have committed arising from the movements of my mind, I now repent before all the Buddhas so that they may be eliminated.
By all the merit I have accumulated through my body, speech, and mind, may it serve as the cause for awakening,
that I may attain the unsurpassed path.
May those who make offerings to the Tathāgatas throughout the lands of the ten directions, as well as the Buddha’s unsurpassed wisdom, [be likewise fulfilled].
I now rejoice in all merits;
I confess every transgression. I rejoice in all this merit; I now pay homage to all Buddhas, vowing to achieve supreme wisdom.
To the great Bodhisattvas of the ten directions who have realized the ten stages, I now prostrate with my head bowed;
may they swiftly realize Bodhi.
Having realized Bodhi, may they subdue the armies of Māra and turn the pure Wheel of Dharma.
Benefiting the multitudes of sentient beings,
may you always remain in the world for immeasurable koṭis of kalpas, beating the great Dharma drum to deliver all suffering beings.
I am submerged in the mire of desire, bound by the cords of craving, and entangled in manifold fetters;
may the Buddha deign to observe me.
Though sentient beings are heavily defiled, the Buddhas never weary of or abandon them; may you look upon me with great compassion.

I now vow to practice and study the bodhisattva path traversed by the present World-Honored Ones who deliver beings from the ocean of birth and death, as well as by the Buddhas of the past and the future.
Fully endowed with the perfections, having accomplished the six supernormal powers, you deliver all sentient beings and realize the unsurpassed path.
You thoroughly understand that all phenomena are empty, signless, devoid of intrinsic nature, non-abiding, and beyond representation.
Neither arising nor ceasing,
like the Great Sage, He has thoroughly realized selflessness, Without a person (pudgala),
and even without a life-principle (jīva).
In all matters of giving, one does not cling to "I" or "mine. For the sake of the peace and happiness of sentient beings, one practices generosity without stinginess, making the vow:
"May the objects I give arise without effort and be understood through the observation of emptiness."
Possessing the perfection of generosity and maintaining precepts without deficiency, one attains the pure śīla of a Buddha; because of non-abiding,
one fulfills the perfection of ethical discipline.
Enduring patience is like the four great elements, Without giving rise to a discriminating mind; Because there is no anger, one fulfills the perfection of patience.
I vow that by the power of body and mind, I shall initiate great vigor, Firm and without indolence.

Possessing the perfection of diligence through [realizing] that all things are like illusions and magical transformations, and through courageous vigor, they possess the perfection of meditation via samādhis such as the vajra-like.
May you realize the wisdom of samādhi and enter the three gates of liberation; May you comprehend the equality of the three times and fulfill the perfection of wisdom;
With the wondrous form-body of all Buddhas, Radiant and of great majestic power, May the bodhisattva practice with diligence.
May I fully accomplish all [perfections].

(This verse is from the *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra*, Chapter 42, "The Questions of Maitreya Bodhisattva. It states that one who bears the name Maitreya diligently cultivates such practices, fulfills the six pāramitās, and dwells securely in the ten stages.)
Having finished speaking, he rises and makes this proclamation.
After performing the dedication and making the vow, he prostrates once in homage to the Triple Gem (one bow),
circumambulates nine times, and takes refuge in himself.

When the ritual is concluded, one rises and adjusts one’s robes. Holding an incense burner in hand, one stands still for a short while, contemplating the Triple Gem and the worthy sages filling the dharma-arena, each seated upon their Dharma throne.
Then, one turns the body in succession, circumambulating each one until all have been passed.
He turned with serene composure, his mouth uttering the Brahma-sound:
"Namo to the Buddhas of the ten directions; namo to the Dharma of the ten directions;
namo to the Sangha of the ten directions; namo to Vairocana Buddha."
Homage to Śākyamuni Buddha; homage to the Buddhas of the three periods throughout the three thousandfold world system;
homage to the "Bodhisattva’s Ground of the Mind" chapter of the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*; homage to Maitreya Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.
Reciting these names either three or seven times, and having completed the circumambulation, return before the image and perform the Three Refuges.
Taking refuge in the Buddha, I vow that all sentient beings shall realize the Great Way and give rise to the unsurpassed mind.
Taking refuge in the Dharma, I vow that all sentient beings shall enter deeply into the treasury of the scriptures, their wisdom as vast as the ocean.
Taking refuge in the Sangha, I vow that all sentient beings shall lead the great assembly, free from all obstacles.
I pay homage to the assembly of noble ones.

Having completed the repentance ritual for those who practice the contemplation of the true nature of reality while seated ten times, one should next proceed to a separate seat, sit upright with the body straightened, close the eyes, and keep the mouth shut.
Regulate the breath, as explained in detail within the preliminary practices for *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.

Next, one should clearly contemplate the offenses previously committed: were they committed due to the mind, due to the object, due to both the mind and the object, or were they committed neither due to the mind nor due to the object? If they were committed due to the mind, that object was not...
At the time when [the object] is present, why is there no offense? If one commits an offense because of the object, then the object itself commits the offense;
it should not be that I commit the offense. Furthermore, if I commit an offense because of the object, then why do the Noble Ones (ārya) not commit offenses regarding objects?
If one commits an offense because of both mind and object, does this mean that the mind and the object each possess the nature of offense, such that an offense occurs only upon their conjunction?

If it were the case that neither the object (*viṣaya*) nor the mind (*citta*) individually possesses the nature of an offense, yet an offense arises only when they coincide, then why would it be necessary to wait for their coincidence?

Furthermore, at the moment of their coincidence, there would be two offenses. If neither the object nor the mind individually possesses the nature of an offense, how could their combination produce one?
It is like a single grain of sand having no oil; how could a multitude of grains of sand ever produce oil? Thus, by way of this cause...
The mind depends on objects; when both mind and object are present, one cannot even find a place where an offense arises.
How much less could an offense arise without depending on the mind or depending on objects? One should know that the nature of offense is fundamentally non-arising.

Because I am deluded and inverted, I falsely conceptualize the existence of mind and the existence of objects within that which is without mind, without objects, and without the nature of either upholding or offending.
Transgressions—such transgressions—are by nature empty and quiescent; they are not empty because they have been extinguished.

Having made this contemplation, one finds nothing to be attained in the mind and nothing to be grasped in objects. One does not perceive the characteristic of the arising of offenses, nor does one perceive the characteristic of their cessation.
It is solely due to the causes and conditions of false and inverted delusion that what is not born appears as if it were born;

because one awakens to the fact that these false and inverted causes and conditions lack intrinsic nature, that which is not extinguished is said to be extinguished. This is called contemplating the emptiness of the nature of transgressions.
If this contemplation is attained and manifests continuously, afflictions will naturally grow thin and the nature of wisdom will gradually open; this is precisely the attainment of the precepts.
This serves as a preliminary introduction. Furthermore, observe this offense: does it exist internally, externally, or in between?
Does it exist in the past, the present, or the future? That which is past has already ceased; that which is present does not abide.
The future does not yet exist; how, then, can there be transgression? Furthermore, consider this transgression: is it created by the body, or is it created by the mind?

If it were created by the body, would it be created by the earth element (*pṛthivī-dhātu*), or by the water, fire, or wind elements (*ab-, tejo-, vāyu-dhātu*), or by the space element (*ākāśa-dhātu*)?
If it is the mind that creates [karma], then what is this mind? Is it blue, yellow, red, or white? Is it long, short, square, or round?
Is it internal, external, or intermediate? Is it past, present, or future? Since the mind has no form, how could it create sin?
Having contemplated in this way, one finds neither a creator nor a created object; it is merely through the perfuming of ignorance that false and deluded [conceptions] arise.
Regarding the inverted causes and conditions: within the nature of neither subject nor object, one illusorily perceives a creator and the created.
Now, observing with correct wisdom as it truly is, both body and mind are empty; thus, there is no master of sin or merit.

It is like frost and dew that the sun of wisdom can dissolve, or like a long-darkened room that a single lamp can shatter. Furthermore, observe this mind: although its fundamental nature is empty, [it continues to manifest].
Quiescent. Without subject and without object; without the mark of sin and without the mark of merit. Because it is without marks, it is unobstructed and boundless, inconceivable.
Transversely pervasive and vertically exhaustive, there is no dharma not contained within it, and no dharma not created by it.
According to whichever single dharma it creates, that very dharma is nonetheless the entire body and great function, which in turn contains all dharmas and in turn creates one.
All phenomena: there is not a single phenomenon that is not an object of creation, nor is there a single phenomenon that is not a creator.

Having contemplated in this way, one deeply penetrates the true nature (*dharmatā*) within the characteristics of transgression. This true nature is precisely the original source, the eternally abiding *dharmakāya* of Buddhahood, and *samādhi*.
If this contemplation is perfected, the essence of the precepts (*śīla-tattva*) will necessarily arise. Therefore, the Sūtra says: "One should..."
One should calmly observe the true nature of all phenomena: they are neither born nor extinguished; neither eternal nor annihilated;
neither identical nor different; neither coming nor going. Thus, within this single mind, one should diligently adorn it through skillful means.
Such practices as those described above are called the "adornment of merit. Such contemplation of principle as described above is called the "adornment of wisdom."

If one possesses the ritual procedures but lacks the contemplation of principle, one cannot purify the source of transgressions. If one possesses the contemplation of principle but lacks the ritual procedures, one cannot exhaust the flow of transgressions.
It is like an old well into which filth has suddenly fallen: the water already present becomes foul and turbid, and the new spring does not flow forth.
In principle, one must draw out the water until it is exhausted and completely remove the silt; only then will the spring’s current become clear and cool.
"Revised and clarified. A question was asked: "The scriptures prescribe that one must perceive auspicious signs (*lakṣaṇa*).

When sitting in meditation, why do you not carefully contemplate the primary and secondary marks (*lakṣaṇānuvyañjana*) of the Buddhas, but instead direct one toward discerning entry into emptiness? The answer was:

"To contemplate the primary and secondary marks of the Buddhas, one must have the root of precepts (*śīlamūla*) purified, as well as a thorough understanding that 'this mind creates the Buddha' and 'this mind is the Buddha.'"

Only then can one cultivate [the practice]. Now, since your precepts have deficiencies and your understanding is likely not yet complete, if you were to focus your mind on visualizing the physical marks, I fear you might invite demonic interference;
therefore, you must certainly wash away the dust of transgressions through the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Question:

The sutras state that by contemplating the Buddha’s marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*), one extinguishes the heavy sins of birth and death accumulated over immeasurable kalpas. How could this not also cleanse the defilements of broken precepts? Answer:

Regarding the contemplation of the physical marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*): it can indeed extinguish transgressions; however, one must possess sharp wisdom and superior faculties to be capable of practicing this sublime contemplation.

Yet, the mere discernment of the emptiness of nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*) is the initial gateway to the Mahāyāna, serving as the direct remedy for the mental defilement of violating the precepts. Question:
Why must Vaidehī and her five hundred female attendants all necessarily possess sharp wisdom and superior faculties? Answer:

It is said: "Vedihi" in the Sanskrit language is translated here as "cultivation through reflection. Is this not sharp wisdom? To be born during the era of a Buddha and personally experience the Buddha’s arrival—is this not a superior faculty?
Question: Among the five methods of cessation and contemplation (*pañca-viṣkambhaṇa*), sentient beings with many obstacles should practice the contemplation of the Buddha.
Why, then, would this instead summon demons? Answer: For those whose retributive obstacles are heavy, it causes them to contemplate the merits of the Buddha.
This serves to eliminate past offenses. Furthermore, it is not necessarily the case that one must single-mindedly contemplate the physical marks (*lakṣaṇa*) [of a Buddha].
If one seeks auspicious signs while current offenses have not yet been eradicated, and both one’s precepts and wisdom are deficient, Māra will surely find an opportunity. Question:

If this is so, then the sūtras should not instruct one to seek auspicious signs. Answer: As for auspicious signs, they cannot be sought with a mind of intentional striving, nor can they be attained through a state of non-striving.
I have gained understanding. Now, one should simply contemplate deeply that the nature of sin is fundamentally empty. Once sin has been eradicated, a spontaneous resonance will arise of itself.
It is like polishing a mirror: when the grime is cleared away, the image appears. Only then does one transcend the two errors of having a mind and having no mind. Question:
The *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* clarifies that for those who cultivate the three contemplations, none of the various realms they hear of should ever be grasped. Now...

Since one has already contemplated that the nature of sin is empty, even if one were to subsequently behold auspicious signs (*lakṣaṇa*), would this not constitute a contradiction between the object and the contemplation? The answer is:
both the ritual and the principle-based methods of repentance aim solely at the extinction of sin; originally, there is no intention to seek after signs.

It is simply because the contemplation of emptiness has become profound that the root of sin is forever uprooted, and through the mutual resonance of the path and its response, these auspicious signs manifest. Although they are seen—
One still realizes the emptiness of nature; therefore, there is no joyful agitation that disturbs the mind, nor is there any alarm that confuses the intent.

Only in this way is it the sign that offenses have been extinguished and the precepts restored. If one perceives auspicious signs while they do not correspond with the contemplation of emptiness, [they are not true signs].

Furthermore, if one’s mind becomes fond of agitation and cannot attain stillness, or if one becomes startled and the mind is distracted such that lightness and ease (*praśrabdhi*) are not obtained, you should know that this is the work of Māra.
You must recognize it clearly and ensure you are not deluded by external conditions.

At that time, you must further penetrate the contemplation of emptiness and maintain the thought that all is but mind-only. If it is the work of Māra, it will surely gradually vanish; if it is truly wholesome, it will persist.
The signs become twice as bright and are able to assist in giving rise to the wisdom of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), causing one to be free from grasping and attachment.

Thus, one knows that the analytical method of discernment possesses great efficacy in extinguishing karmic obstructions and hindrances; it is easy for those at the initial stage of practice to enter, allowing them to sweep away the beginningless false attachments to the self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-grāha*) and to suddenly attain the true principle of the *dharmatā* of the Mahāyāna. If a practitioner can act in this way...

Regarding the two types of repentance—of phenomena and of principle—one should practice them with diligent perseverance. Not only do they extinguish transgressions, but there are also differing signs of realization according to the three faculties.
For those of inferior faculty, the purity of the precepts is first attained. This, in turn, has three grades. First, the inferior grade:

one obtains auspicious dreams, and upon waking, perceives that the sense organs are clear and pure, the four elements are light and at ease, and the aspiration for the Way increases. Second, the middling grade...

As for the practitioner, within the state of seated meditation, they behold various auspicious omens, radiant splendors, extraordinary fragrances, and the sound of virtuous praise; thus they attain the joy of the Dharma.

Regarding the three superior grades: within a tranquil mind, they personally see their own physical form as dignified and majestic, their deportment flawless, and the characteristics of the *pātimokkha* precepts manifesting in succession;
they abide in peace and security, free from fear. Those of middling faculties realize meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
There are three grades of purity: either the purity of the category of wisdom (*jñāna-viśuddhi*) is realized by those of superior faculties; or one gives rise to mundane pure dhyāna;
or one gives rise to dhyāna that is both mundane and supramundane; or again, one gives rise to supramundane dhyāna. These constitute the three grades.

As for the realization of the purity of the category of wisdom by those of superior faculties—whether they give rise to contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-caryā*), reach the stage of semblance (*sādṛśya-bhūmi*), or enter the stage of partial truth (*praveśa-tattva-bhūmi*)—this is explained extensively in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and other texts concerning samādhis.
The Ritual for Repentance According to the Brahmajāla Sūtra (End)
